title: The Macartney Embassy to the Qianlong Emperor
intro: Viscount Macartney led the first British diplomatic mission to China, with about a hundred people. It sailed from Britain in 1792 to ask for new ports for British trade, a permanent embassy in Beijing, a small island for British use and fewer restrictions on trade at Canton.
ending: The Qianlong Emperor rejected all of the mission's requests. The embassy returned to London without obtaining any concession from China, but it brought back detailed observations of the empire.

stops.text: The delegation sailed from Portsmouth in three ships: HMS Lion, the East Indiaman Hindostan and the brig Jackall. Captain Sir Erasmus Gower commanded the Lion, which led the mission.
stops.quote: The delegation departed Portsmouth aboard three ships on 26 September 1792.

stops.text: A storm struck the squadron soon after it left and forced it to stop at Torbay for repairs. The Jackall went missing in the storm, and the Lion and Hindostan went on without her.
stops.quote: A storm soon hit the squadron, forcing it to stop temporarily at Torbay.

stops.text: The squadron stopped at Madeira in early October, and at the Canary Islands later in the same month.
stops.quote: The squadron stopped at Madeira in early October, and at the Canary Islands later that same month.

stops.text: The ships arrived at Porto Praya in Cape Verde and waited five days for the Jackall. The crews of the Lion and Hindostan believed she was wrecked, and the squadron sailed on without her.
stops.quote: On 1 November, they arrived at Porto Praya in Cape Verde. After waiting five days for Jackall, they continued on their journey.

stops.text: The trade winds off the coast of Africa forced the ships to sail west to Rio de Janeiro, which they reached at the end of November. Macartney had an attack of gout there that lasted a month.
stops.quote: The trade winds off the coast of Africa forced them to sail west all the way to Rio de Janeiro, where they arrived at the end of November.

stops.text: The expedition left Rio de Janeiro on 17 December, sailed east again and rounded the Cape of Good Hope.
stops.quote: The expedition departed Rio de Janeiro on 17 December and sailed east once more, rounding the Cape of Good Hope on 7 January 1793.

stops.text: The squadron passed Java in February and reached Batavia. There the embassy bought a French brig and named her Clarence, and the Jackall, which had turned back for repairs, rejoined the squadron.
stops.quote: They passed Java in February and reached Batavia on 6 March. There, they bought a French brig which they christened Clarence, to replace Jackall.

stops.text: The embassy anchored at Tourane until 16 June and visited Tây Sơn-ruled Cochinchina, where it received gifts from the emperor Cảnh Thịnh. Local people arrested the master of the Lion and seven other men and released them a week later.
stops.quote: From 26 May to 16 June, the embassy anchored at Tourane and visited Tây Sơn-ruled Cochinchina where they received gifts from emperor Cảnh Thịnh.

stops.text: The full squadron arrived at Macau. George Staunton went ashore to meet East India Company officials, and three of the four Chinese Catholic priests left the mission, leaving one Chinese interpreter.
stops.quote: The full squadron sailed on to Macau, where they arrived on 19 June 1793. There, George Staunton disembarked to meet with officials of the East India Company.

legs.title: North along the coast and up the Hai River

stops.text: After leaving Macao on 23 June the embassy stopped at Zhoushan, where Staunton went ashore to meet the military governor of Dinghai. The governor supplied pilots, as the Emperor had ordered every port to do.
stops.quote: The embassy departed Macao on 23 June. It stopped in Zhoushan, where Staunton went ashore to meet with the military governor of Dinghai.

stops.text: Macartney and his group went on to Dagu in the smallest ships. There he and Staunton met Liang Kentang, Viceroy of Zhili, who told them the Emperor would receive them at Rehe (Jehol) rather than in Beijing.
stops.quote: Macartney and his group continued separately to Dagu on the smallest British ships, the Jackall, the Clarence, and the Endeavour. On 6 August, Macartney and Staunton met with Liang Kentang (梁肯堂), Viceroy of Zhili, who had traveled from Baoding to see them.

stops.text: Macartney and Staunton attended a banquet with Viceroy Liang and the Manchu legate Zhengrui. Macartney persuaded the viceroy to let some of the gifts stay in Beijing to avoid damage on the journey to Rehe.
stops.quote: The embassy continued to Tianjin, where it arrived on 11 August.

stops.text: The mission went up the Hai River in small boats pulled by men along the shore with ropes and harnesses, and landed at Tongzhou.
stops.quote: The mission continued up the Hai River on small boats pulled by men along the shore using ropes and harnesses. It landed at Tongzhou on 16 August.

legs.title: Beijing, the Great Wall and Chengde

stops.text: The embassy was escorted to a residence near the Old Summer Palace and not permitted to leave it. The gifts were stored in the throne room there, and the planetarium took 18 days to assemble.
stops.quote: The embassy reached Beijing on 21 August. It was escorted to a residence north of Beijing, near the Old Summer Palace. The British were not permitted to leave the premises for the duration of their stay.

stops.text: About seventy members of the mission, forty of them soldiers, left Beijing on 2 September and crossed the Great Wall at Gubeikou. Lieutenant Parish surveyed the Wall's fortifications, which aroused suspicion among their hosts.
stops.quote: The group crossed the Great Wall of China at Gubeikou, where they were greeted by ceremonial gunfire and several companies of troops from the Eight Banners of the Qing military.

stops.text: The entourage reached the outskirts of Chengde, where the Qianlong Emperor awaited them. The same day an edict allowed Macartney a single prostration in place of the usual nine.
stops.quote: The entourage arrived at the outskirts of Chengde on 8 September.

stops.text: Macartney met the Qianlong Emperor in the imperial tent. After a dispute over the kowtow, it was agreed that he would genuflect on one knee, and he presented King George III's letter and exchanged gifts with the Emperor.
stops.quote: Here too, Macartney's embassy was to meet Qianlong on the occasion of the Emperor's birthday.

notes: The article gives the way out in detail but says nothing of the return journey (no places or dates between the audience and the embassy's arrival in London), so the route ends at Chengde and the ending line carries the return. The way back through China to Canton is not in the article and is left out. Torbay and Zhoushan: the article gives no day, so the date is the year or month. Zhoushan: the 23 June departure is in the quote; the stop itself is undated beyond the June departure. Chengde appears twice (arrival 8 September, audience 14 September). Dagu: the article places the mouth of the Hai River on 25 July (anchored, muddy water) but names Dagu only for the transfer of gifts and Macartney's onward journey; wp 'Dagu District' is the nearest town-level article and the editor should check the point. Tongzhou wp title 'Tongzhou District, Beijing' to check. Batavia entry jakarta is the same site under its later name; Tourane likewise da-nang. The Lion and Hindostan were sent back to Zhoushan and Guangzhou but the article gives no route for them. Left out: Canary Islands (named only in passing, no event), Java (passed), Old Summer Palace (inside the Beijing stop). The article says 1793 for the mission; the years 1792–1794 are the dates of the voyage given in the article's further reading.
